body.en:
Definition: An array is a fixed-size, sequenced collection of elements of the same data type, stored in contiguous (adjacent) memory locations and accessed by a common name with an index (subscript).

Need for arrays

To store the marks of 60 students we would need 60 separate variables, which is impractical. An array stores all of them under one name:

/* Without array: 5 variables */
int m1, m2, m3, m4, m5;

/* With array: one name */
int m[5];

With an array, a loop can read, process and print all elements using the index.

Characteristics of arrays

  • All elements are of the same data type (homogeneous).
  • Elements are stored in contiguous memory locations.
  • The size is fixed at declaration and cannot be changed at run time.
  • The index starts at 0; the last index is size − 1.
  • Any element can be accessed directly by its index (random access).
  • The array name holds the base address (address of the first element).
  • C does not check array bounds.

Types of arrays (see diagram)

  1. One-dimensional (1-D) – a list, e.g. int a[5];
  2. Two-dimensional (2-D) – a table/matrix, e.g. int m[3][4];
  3. Multi-dimensional – three or more dimensions, e.g. int x[2][3][4];

Advantages and disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Many values under one nameFixed size: memory may be wasted or be insufficient
Easy processing with loopsOnly one data type
Fast random access by indexInsertion/deletion needs shifting
Used for sorting, searching, matricesNo bounds checking

A list of items that is given one variable name and uses only one subscript is called a one-dimensional array. For example, a[5] contains five elements: a[0], a[1], a[2], a[3], a[4].

Memory representation (see diagram)

For int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; with base address 1000 and 4-byte int, the elements are at 1000, 1004, 1008, 1012 and 1016.

Address of a[i] = Base address + i × sizeof(data type)

Example: address of a[3] = 1000 + 3 × 4 = 1012.

Total memory = size × sizeof(data type) = 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.

Accessing elements

a[0] = 5;             /* first element */
a[n - 1] = 9;         /* last element */
x = a[2] + a[3];
a[i]++;

The subscript can be any integer expression: a constant, a variable or an expression such as a[i+1].

No bounds checking

int a[5];
/* no compiler error, but outside the array! */
a[5] = 100;

C does not check whether an index is inside the array. Writing outside the array can overwrite other data or crash the program, so the programmer must keep the index between 0 and size−1.

Like any other variable, an array must be declared before it is used, so that the compiler can allocate memory.

Syntax

data_type array_name[size];
  • data_type – type of each element (int, float, char, …).
  • array_name – a valid identifier.
  • size – maximum number of elements; must be a positive integer constant (or a symbolic constant).

Examples

/* 60 integers  = 240 bytes */
int   marks[60];
/* 10 floats    = 40 bytes  */
float price[10];
/* 20 characters = 20 bytes */
char  name[20];

#define N 100
/* symbolic constant as size */
int roll[N];

Invalid declarations

/* error: size missing */
int a[];
/* VLA: C99 only, avoid in Turbo C */
int n = 5; int b[n];
/* error: negative size */
int c[-5];
/* error: size must be integer */
int d[2.5];

Note: a character array (string) must have one extra place for the null character '\0'. To store "GTU" we need char s[4].

Storing initial values in an array is called initialization. An array can be initialized at compile time or at run time. An uninitialized local array contains garbage values.

1. Compile-time initialization

Syntax: data_type array_name[size] = {list of values};

/* full */
int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
/* partial: 1 2 0 0 0 */
int b[5] = {1, 2};
/* all elements 0 */
int c[5] = {0};
/* size taken as 4 */
int d[]  = {4, 8, 15, 16};
/* character array */
char s[] = {'G', 'T', 'U', '\0'};
/* same, size 4 */
char t[] = "GTU";
  • Values are separated by commas and enclosed in braces.
  • If fewer values than the size are given, the remaining elements are set to 0 (partial initialization).
  • If the size is omitted, the compiler takes the number of values as the size.
  • Giving more values than the size is an error:
/* error: too many */
int e[3] = {1, 2, 3, 4};

2. Run-time initialization

Values are given while the program runs, using scanf() or assignment inside a loop. This is used for large arrays or values entered by the user.

for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    scanf("%d", &a[i]);

/* assign by formula */
for (i = 0; i < 100; i++)
    sq[i] = i * i;

Common operations performed on 1-D arrays:

OperationMeaningLogic
TraversalVisit every element once (print, sum, count)for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
Largest / smallestFind the max or min elementStart with a[0], compare with the rest
SearchingFind whether an item is present and whereLinear search: compare one by one
SortingArrange in ascending/descending orderBubble sort: swap adjacent pairs
InsertionAdd an element at a positionShift elements right, then insert
DeletionRemove an element from a positionShift elements left
ReversalReverse the order of elementsSwap a[i] with a[n-1-i]

Linear search algorithm (see flowchart)

  1. Read n, the elements and the key.
  2. Set i = 0.
  3. If i < n is false, print "Not found" and stop.
  4. If a[i] == key, print "Found at i" and stop.
  5. i = i + 1; go to step 3.

Bubble sort algorithm

  1. Repeat for pass i = 0 to n−2:
  2.   Repeat for j = 0 to n−2−i: if a[j] > a[j+1], swap them.
  3. Print the sorted array.

See the diagram "Bubble Sort – Pass by Pass" for a traced example.

Bubble sort is the simplest sorting technique. In each pass, adjacent elements are compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order. After every pass the largest remaining element moves ("bubbles") to its correct position at the end.

Example: 50 20 40 10 30 (see diagram)

PassResultComparisons
120 40 10 30 504
220 10 30 40 503
310 20 30 40 502
410 20 30 40 501
  • For n elements: n − 1 passes; pass i needs n − 1 − i comparisons.
  • Total comparisons = n(n − 1)/2 = 10 for n = 5.
  • Swapping uses a temporary variable: temp = a[j]; a[j] = a[j+1]; a[j+1] = temp;

An array with two subscripts is called a two-dimensional array. It stores data in the form of a table (matrix) with rows and columns, e.g. the marks of 60 students in 5 subjects.

In m[i][j], the first subscript i is the row and the second subscript j is the column. Both start at 0.

Memory representation – row-major order (see diagram)

Memory is linear, so C stores a 2-D array row by row: all elements of row 0, then row 1, and so on. This is called row-major order.

Address of a[i][j] = Base + (i × number_of_columns + j) × size

Example: int m[2][3], base 1000 → address of m[1][2] = 1000 + (1×3 + 2)×4 = 1020.

Total memory = rows × columns × size = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 bytes.

Applications

Matrices (addition, multiplication, transpose), tables of marks/sales, games boards, images (pixels).

Syntax

data_type array_name[row_size][column_size];
  • row_size – number of rows; column_size – number of columns.
  • Each size is written in a separate pair of brackets. int m[3,4]; is wrong.
  • Total elements = row_size × column_size.

Examples

/* 3 rows, 4 columns = 12 ints = 48 bytes */
int   m[3][4];
/* 60 students x 5 subjects */
float marks[60][5];

Elements of int m[3][4]: m[0][0] … m[0][3], m[1][0] … m[1][3], m[2][0] … m[2][3].

1. Compile-time initialization

/* 1. Row-wise with inner braces (recommended) */
int a[2][3] = { {1, 2, 3},
                {4, 5, 6} };

/* 2. Without inner braces – filled row by row */
int b[2][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};

/* 3. Partial – missing elements become 0 */
/* 1 0 0 / 4 5 0 */
int c[2][3] = { {1}, {4, 5} };

/* 4. First dimension may be omitted */
int d[][3] = { {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6} };

/* 5. All zero */
int z[3][3] = {0};
  • Inner braces make each row clear; elements not given become 0.
  • The first dimension (rows) may be omitted; the column size is compulsory, because the compiler needs it to know where each row ends.

2. Run-time initialization

Nested loops are used: the outer loop for rows, the inner loop for columns.

for (i = 0; i < r; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < c; j++)
        scanf("%d", &a[i][j]);

To print in matrix form, put printf("\n") after the inner loop.

OperationConditionFormulaResult order
AdditionSame orderc[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j]m × n
SubtractionSame orderc[i][j] = a[i][j] - b[i][j]m × n
Multiplicationcols of A = rows of Bc[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]m × p
TransposeAnyt[j][i] = a[i][j]n × m
Diagonal sumSquare matrixif (i == j) sum += a[i][j]–

Matrix multiplication (see diagram)

Each element C[i][j] is the sum of products of row i of A and column j of B, so three nested loops are needed:

for (i = 0; i < m; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < p; j++)
    {
        c[i][j] = 0;
        for (k = 0; k < n; k++)
            c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
    }

• Array = fixed-size collection of same-type elements in contiguous memory, accessed by index.
  • Index: 0 to size−1. C does no bounds checking.
  • 1-D: int a[5]; address = base + i × size; memory = n × size.
  • Initialization: {10, 20} → rest 0; int d[] = {…} → size from list; run time with a loop + scanf.
  • 2-D: int m[r][c]; stored in row-major order; address = base + (i × c + j) × size.
  • 2-D initialization: row size may be omitted, column size is compulsory.
  • Bubble sort: n−1 passes, adjacent swaps. Linear search: compare one by one.
  • Matrix multiplication needs cols(A) = rows(B) and 3 nested loops.

Computer memory is a sequence of storage cells (bytes), and each byte has a unique number called its address. When a variable is declared, the compiler reserves memory for it at some address.

Definition: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable.

/* x: value 25, stored at (say) 1000 */
int x = 25;
/* p: value 1000 = address of x     */
int *p = &x;

Since p contains the address of x, we say "p points to x" (see diagram). A pointer variable has its own address too (here 2000).

Why pointers? (Applications)

  • Access and change variables indirectly (e.g. swap via functions – call by reference).
  • Return more than one value from a function.
  • Efficient handling of arrays and strings.
  • Dynamic memory allocation (malloc, calloc).
  • Building data structures: linked lists, trees, stacks.
  • File handling (FILE pointers, Unit 5).

• A pointer stores an address, not an ordinary value.
  • Every pointer has a type: an int * points to an int, a float * to a float. The type tells the compiler how many bytes to read at that address.
  • The size of a pointer is the same for all types on a given system (4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 bytes on 64-bit), because it stores only an address.
  • & gives the address of a variable; * gives the value at an address.
  • A pointer must be initialized before use; otherwise it is a wild pointer with a garbage address.
  • Pointer arithmetic is allowed: p + 1 moves to the next element (address + sizeof(type)).
  • The array name is a constant pointer to the first element.
  • A pointer can point to another pointer (pointer to pointer, int **q).
  • Special types: void pointer (generic) and NULL pointer (points nowhere).

Advantages and disadvantages

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Faster, efficient array/string handlingUninitialized pointers cause crashes
Call by reference; return many valuesHard to understand and debug
Dynamic memory allocationMemory leaks if memory is not freed
Data structures (lists, trees)Can corrupt other data by wrong addresses

h.en: 3.2.3 Address of Operator (&) and Indirection Operator (*)

body.en:
1. Address of operator ( & )

The unary operator & returns the memory address of its operand. It is read as "address of". %p is used to print an address.

int x = 25;
printf("%d\n", x);          /* 25 */
printf("%p\n", (void *) &x); /* address */
/* & passes the address */
scanf("%d", &x);

& can be used only with variables and array elements, not with constants or expressions:

/* error: constant has no address  */
&125
/* error: expression has no address */
&(a + b)
int arr[5];
/* allowed, but arr alone is already an address */
&arr

2. Indirection operator ( * )

The unary operator *, applied to a pointer, gives the value stored at the address the pointer holds. It is read as "value at address" and is also called the dereference operator.

int x = 25, y;
int *p = &x;
/* y = 25   (read through pointer)  */
y = *p;
/* x = 40   (write through pointer) */
*p = 40;

Relation between & and *

ExpressionValue (x = 25 at 1000, p = &x at 2000)
x25
&x1000
p1000
*p25
&p2000
*&x25 (* and & cancel)

Note: the * in a declaration (int *p;) only says that p is a pointer; the * in an expression (*p) means "value at".

Declaration

Syntax:

data_type *pointer_name;
  • * tells the compiler that the variable is a pointer.
  • data_type is the type of the variable the pointer will point to.
int   *ip;        /* pointer to int   */
float *fp;        /* pointer to float */
char  *cp;        /* pointer to char  */
int   *a, *b;     /* two pointers */
/* c is pointer, d is int! */
int   *c, d;

Initialization

Assigning the address of a variable to a pointer is called pointer initialization. The variable must be declared before its address is taken.

int x = 10;
int *p;
/* initialization by assignment */
p = &x;

int y = 20;
/* declaration + initialization */
int *q = &y;

/* points nowhere (safe) */
int *r = NULL;
/* copy of another pointer */
int *s = q;

Rules / common errors

float f = 2.5;
int *p = &f;      /* wrong: type mismatch */
/* wrong: integer is not an address */
int *q = 1000;
int *w;
/* wrong: wild pointer, garbage address */
*w = 5;
  • The data type of the pointer and the variable must match.
  • Never use *p before p holds a valid address.
  • If no address is available yet, initialize with NULL.

Pointer to pointer

A pointer that stores the address of another pointer is declared with two stars (see diagram):

int x = 25;
int *p = &x;
int **q = &p;     /* pointer to pointer */
printf("%d", **q);  /* 25 */

The name of an array is the address of its first element: a == &a[0]. So a pointer can be set to an array and moved through it.

int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int *p = a;       /* p = &a[0] */
/* now p = &a[1]  (address + 4) */
p++;
printf("%d", *p);       /* 20 */
printf("%d", *(p + 2)); /* 40 */

Allowed pointer operations

  • p + n, p - n, p++, p--: move n elements forward/back. The address changes by n × sizeof(type).
  • p2 - p1: number of elements between two pointers into the same array.
  • Comparison p1 < p2, p == NULL.

Not allowed

Adding two pointers (p1 + p2), multiplying or dividing pointers, adding a float to a pointer.

Equivalent notations (see diagram)

a[i] ≡ *(a + i) ≡ *(p + i) ≡ p[i] and &a[i] ≡ a + i

A void pointer is a generic pointer declared with type void. It can hold the address of a variable of any data type.

Syntax: void *pointer_name;

void *vp;
int n = 5;
vp = &n;
/* cast before * */
printf("%d", *(int *) vp);

Features

  • One void pointer can point to int, float, char, … at different times.
  • It cannot be dereferenced directly; it must first be type-cast to the proper pointer type: *(float *) vp.
  • Pointer arithmetic is not allowed on void pointers (the size of the data is unknown).
  • Used in generic functions: malloc() and calloc() return void *; memcpy() and qsort() take void pointers.

A NULL pointer is a pointer that does not point to any valid memory location. It is created by assigning the constant NULL (defined in <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, value 0).

Syntax: data_type *pointer_name = NULL;

/* NULL is defined here */
#include <stdio.h>
int *p = NULL;
if (p != NULL)
    printf("%d", *p);  /* safe */

Uses

  • To initialize a pointer when no address is available yet (avoids wild pointers).
  • To check whether a pointer is valid before dereferencing it.
  • Functions return NULL to signal failure: malloc() when memory is not available, fopen() when a file cannot be opened (Unit 5).
  • To mark the end of linked lists.

Dereferencing a NULL pointer gives a run-time error (segmentation fault).

Comparison of special pointers

PointerMeaningSafe to use *?
void pointerGeneric pointer to any typeOnly after casting
NULL pointerPoints to nothing (value 0)No – check first
Wild pointerUninitialized, garbage addressNo – always initialize
Dangling pointerPoints to memory that was freed or no longer existsNo – set to NULL after free

void pointer vs NULL pointer: void is a type of pointer (generic), whereas NULL is a value of a pointer (no address). A void pointer can also be NULL.

• Pointer = variable that stores the address of another variable: int *p = &x;
  • & address-of operator; * indirection (value-at) operator; *&x == x.
  • Declare: type *name; – the pointer type must match the variable type.
  • Pointer size is the same for all types (8 bytes on 64-bit). Print addresses with %p.
  • p + 1 moves by sizeof(type); a[i] ≡ *(a + i).
  • void pointer: generic, cast before * (*(int *)vp).
  • NULL pointer: points nowhere; check if (p != NULL) before use.
  • Wild pointer = uninitialized; dangling pointer = points to freed memory.

title.en: Read N elements, print them with sum and average

programs.out:
How many elements? 5
Enter 5 elements: 12 45 7 23 56
Elements: 12 45 7 23 56 
Sum = 143
Average = 28.60

expl.en:
• int a[50] reserves space for up to 50 integers; only the first n are used.
  • The elements are read at run time with a for loop. &a[i] is the address of the i-th element.
  • Index runs from 0 to n-1, so the loop condition is i < n.
  • (float) sum / n avoids integer division: 143 / 5 = 28.60.

title.en: Largest and smallest element of an array

programs.out:
How many elements? 6
Enter 6 elements: 34 -8 91 17 0 56
Largest = 91
Smallest = -8

expl.en: The first element is taken as both the largest and the smallest. Every other element is then compared with them and replaces them if it is bigger or smaller. Starting with a[0] instead of 0 makes the program work for negative numbers as well.

programs.out:
How many elements? 6
Enter 6 elements: 15 42 8 23 4 16
Enter element to search: 23
23 found at index 3 (position 4)

expl.en:
Linear (sequential) search compares the key with each element, starting at index 0, until a match is found or the array ends (see flowchart).

  • pos = -1 means "not found yet"; -1 can never be a valid index.
  • Index 3 is the 4th position, because indexing starts at 0.
  • Worst case: n comparisons. It works on unsorted arrays.

programs.out:
How many elements? 5
Enter 5 elements: 50 20 40 10 30
Sorted array: 10 20 30 40 50

expl.en:
• The outer loop makes n-1 passes. In each pass the inner loop compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
  • After pass 1 the largest element is at the end, so each later pass checks one element fewer (n - 1 - i).
  • The diagram "Bubble Sort – Pass by Pass" traces this exact input.
  • For descending order, change > to <.

title.en: Reverse the elements of an array (in place)

expl.en:
• Compile-time initialization with the size omitted: the compiler counts 6 values and makes a[6].
  • sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) = 24 / 4 = 6 gives the number of elements.
  • Element i is swapped with element n-1-i. Only n/2 swaps are needed; going further would reverse the array back.

title.en: Insert an element at a given position

programs.out:
Enter element and position (1 to 6): 25 3
Array after insertion: 10 20 25 30 40 50

expl.en: An array has a fixed size and its elements are contiguous, so to insert in the middle, the elements from the end down to the position are shifted one place to the right. The shift starts from the last element so that no value is overwritten. Position 3 means index 2.

title.en: Read and display a matrix (2-D array)

programs.out:
Initialized matrix t:
   1   2   3
   4   5   6
Enter rows and columns: 3 3
Enter 9 elements row-wise:
1 0 2
4 5 6
7 8 9
Matrix m:
   1   0   2
   4   5   6
   7   8   9

expl.en:
• A 2-D array is processed with nested loops: the outer loop selects the row i, the inner loop the column j.
  • %4d gives each number a width of 4, so the columns line up.
  • printf("\n") after the inner loop starts a new row.

programs.out:
Enter rows and columns: 2 3
Enter matrix A:
1 2 3
4 5 6
Enter matrix B:
6 5 4
3 2 1
Sum matrix:
   7   7   7
   7   7   7

expl.en: Matrices can be added only if they have the same order (rows × columns). Each element of the result is s[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j]. For subtraction, change + to −.

programs.out:
Enter rows and columns of A: 2 2
Enter rows and columns of B: 2 2
Enter matrix A:
1 2
3 4
Enter matrix B:
5 6
7 8
Product matrix:
   19   22
   43   50

expl.en:
• Condition: columns of A = rows of B (n = p). The result has order m × q.
  • Each element c[i][j] is the sum of the products of row i of A and column j of B, so a third loop (k) is needed.
  • c[i][j] must be set to 0 before adding the products.
  • See the diagram "Matrix Multiplication": C[0][0] = 1×5 + 2×7 = 19.
In the transpose the rows become columns: t[j][i] = a[i][j]. A 3 × 4 matrix gives a 4 × 3 transpose, so a separate array t of the opposite order is used.

title.en: Sum of diagonal elements and row sums of a square matrix

programs.out:
Sum of row 0 = 7
Sum of row 1 = 15
Sum of row 2 = 23
Sum of main diagonal = 18

expl.en: The elements of the main diagonal have equal row and column index (i == j): 4 + 5 + 9 = 18. The row sum is reset to 0 at the start of each row. (Secondary diagonal: i + j == n - 1.)

programs.out:
Value of x      = 25
Address of x    = 0x7ffe727b6a3c
Value of p      = 0x7ffe727b6a3c
Value at *p     = 25
Address of p    = 0x7ffe727b6a30
After *p = 40, x = 40
sizeof(p) = 8 bytes

expl.en:
• &x (address-of operator) gives the memory address of x. It is stored in pointer p.
  • *p (indirection / dereference operator) gives the value at that address, i.e. 25.
  • *p = 40; changes x itself, because p points to x.
  • %p prints an address in hexadecimal. The addresses differ on every computer and run.
  • On a 64-bit system every pointer is 8 bytes, whatever type it points to.

programs.out:
Enter two numbers: 15 40
After swap: a = 40, b = 15

expl.en:
• int *pa = &a; declares and initializes a pointer in one statement.
  • scanf("%d", pa) needs no &, because pa already contains the address of a.
  • The swap is done through *pa and *pb, so the original variables a and b change. This idea is used in Unit 4 for call by reference.

title.en: Access array elements using a pointer

expl.en:
• The array name a is the address of its first element, so p = a is valid.
  • Pointer arithmetic: p + i points to the i-th element after p. The address increases by i × sizeof(int), not by i bytes.
  • *(p + i) is the same as a[i] and p[i].
  • Subtracting two pointers gives the number of elements between them.

programs.out:
int   value = 10
float value = 2.5
char  value = A

expl.en:
• A void pointer can store the address of a variable of any data type.
  • It cannot be dereferenced directly (the compiler does not know the size of the data), so it must first be type-cast: *(int *) vp.
  • Pointer arithmetic is not allowed on void pointers in standard C.
  • Library functions such as malloc() return void *.

programs.out:
p is NULL - not dereferenced
p points to x, *p = 7
p reset to NULL: null

expl.en:
• A NULL pointer holds the value NULL (0), meaning it points to no valid memory.
  • Initializing a pointer to NULL avoids a wild pointer (an uninitialized pointer holding a garbage address).
  • Always check if (p != NULL) before using *p. Dereferencing NULL crashes the program (segmentation fault).
  • In a condition, a NULL pointer is false, so p ? … : … works.

q.en: What is an array?

a.en: A fixed-size collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations and accessed using a common name and an index.

q.en: What is the starting index of an array in C?

a.en: 0. The last index is size − 1.

q.en: Why are arrays needed?

a.en: To store many values of the same type under one name and process them easily with loops, instead of using many separate variables.

q.en: What happens if fewer values are given during initialization?

a.en: The remaining elements are automatically set to 0.

q.en: Can the size of an array be omitted?

a.en: Yes, if the array is initialized; the compiler takes the number of values as the size, e.g. int a[] = {1, 2, 3};

q.en: What is the value of elements of an uninitialized local array?

a.en: Garbage (unpredictable) values.

q.en: Does C check array bounds?

a.en: No. Accessing outside the bounds gives unpredictable results or a crash; the programmer must ensure valid indexes.

q.en: How many bytes does int a[10] occupy?

a.en: 10 × sizeof(int) = 40 bytes (with 4-byte int; 20 bytes in Turbo C).

q.en: How do you find the number of elements of an array?

a.en: sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]).

q.en: What is a two-dimensional array?

a.en: An array with two subscripts (rows and columns) that stores data in table/matrix form.

q.en: What is row-major order?

a.en: Storing a 2-D array row by row in memory: all elements of row 0 first, then row 1, and so on. C uses row-major order.

q.en: Which dimension can be omitted while initializing a 2-D array?

a.en: Only the first (row) dimension; the column size must always be given.

q.en: What is the condition for matrix multiplication?

a.en: The number of columns of the first matrix must equal the number of rows of the second matrix.

q.en: How many passes does bubble sort need for n elements?

a.en: n − 1 passes.

q.en: What is linear search?

a.en: Searching by comparing the key with each element one by one from the beginning until it is found or the array ends.

q.en: What is a pointer?

a.en: A variable that stores the memory address of another variable.

q.en: What is the use of the & operator?

a.en: It is the address-of operator; it returns the memory address of a variable.

q.en: What is the use of the * operator with pointers?

a.en: In a declaration it marks a pointer; in an expression it is the indirection (dereference) operator that gives the value at the address.

q.en: How do you declare a pointer to float?

a.en: float *fp;

q.en: Which format specifier prints an address?
What is the size of a pointer?

a.en: It is the same for all data types: 4 bytes on 32-bit systems and 8 bytes on 64-bit systems (2 bytes in 16-bit Turbo C).

q.en: What is a wild pointer?

a.en: A pointer that has been declared but not initialized, so it holds a garbage address.

q.en: What is a NULL pointer?

a.en: A pointer assigned the value NULL (0) that points to no valid memory location.

q.en: What is a void pointer?

a.en: A generic pointer (void *) that can hold the address of any data type; it must be type-cast before dereferencing.

q.en: Can we dereference a void pointer directly?

a.en: No, it must first be cast to a specific pointer type, e.g. *(int *)vp.

q.en: What is a dangling pointer?

a.en: A pointer that still points to a memory location that has been freed or no longer exists.

q.en: What is a pointer to pointer?

a.en: A pointer that stores the address of another pointer, declared like int **q;

q.en: What does p + 1 mean if p is an int pointer?

a.en: It points to the next integer, i.e. the address increases by sizeof(int) bytes.

q.en: What is the relation between arrays and pointers?

a.en: The array name is the address of the first element, so a[i] is the same as *(a + i).

q.en: Can two pointers be added?

a.en: No. Pointers can be subtracted (if they point into the same array) and compared, but not added, multiplied or divided.
